Press enter or click to view image in full size A few years ago, writing a Product Requirements Document (PRD) meant defining the problem, aligning stakeholders, documenting requirements, and securing buy-in before development began. That process still matters. But AI is changing how we approach it. When prototypes can be built in hours instead of weeks, why spend weeks documenting a solution before testing whether it works? The better approach is to explore multiple solutions, select the strongest one, and write the PRD around the decision. Here is what a modern AI-era PRD should include. Press enter or click to view image in full size 1. The decision Which solution are we shipping, why did we choose it, and what alternatives did we consider? 2. The opportunity Define the user problem, supporting data, user feedback, hypothesis, and strategic fit. 3. The prototype Link the selected prototype. Let the working experience demonstrate the solution instead of relying on lengthy descriptions. 4. The behavior contract For AI features, document 15–25 representative examples covering expected responses, incorrect outputs, ambiguous inputs, edge cases, and appropriate refusals. 5. Success metrics and AI evaluations Define measurable product outcomes, guardrails, and an offline evaluation dataset before launch. Use human review where needed to verify output quality. 6. Scope and non-goals Be explicit about what is included, what is excluded, and which trade-offs the team is willing to accept. 7. Rollout and rollback Specify exposure limits, rollout stages, success thresholds, rollback conditions, and who is responsible for stopping the release. 8. Release criteria and learning Define what qualifies as done. After launch, add the results, unexpected findings, and the decision to iterate, scale, or retire the feature. The bigger shift AI makes it easier to generate prototypes, requirements, and code. But producing more does not automatically mean building better products. The product manager’s job is to reduce uncertainty, challenge assumptions, evaluate trade-offs, and ensure that what ships creates measurable value. The PRD is still an essential product management tool. Its role is evolving from documenting everything upfront to capturing the reasoning, expected behavior, success criteria, and decisions that guide a product throughout its lifecycle. Prototype with curiosity. Document with clarity. Ship with evidence. For AI product managers, that is a practical place to start. What would you add to a modern AI-era PRD?
